A link protocol for the WAN

HDLC is a data link layer WAN protocol that is bit-oriented. Older protocols were character-oriented: special characters marked the start and end, and if the message contained one of them it was executed as an action and the message ended up truncated.

It was created to handle two scenarios:

  • Unbalanced: one primary station (the host: maintains the link and issues commands) and secondary terminals, which only issue responses.
  • Balanced: two combined stations, which issue both commands and responses. This is the one used today, for example between two routers connected by a serial link.
From here on we work with two combined stations on a point-to-point link.

The physical layer delivers a sequence of bits; the data link layer has to detect where each frame starts and ends. In HDLC this is marked by a flag: 01111110 (7E in hexadecimal).

This imposes a restriction: the flag cannot appear inside the message. The sender scans what it is going to send and after five consecutive 1s inserts a 0, regardless of what comes next.

The receiver does the opposite: when it finds five consecutive 1s, it removes the 0 that follows and rebuilds the original message.
Thanks to zero insertion the transmission is transparent: the message can contain any combination of bits.
The example message starts with exactly 01111110. The two orange 0s are added by the sender and removed by the receiver: on the link there are never six consecutive 1s, except in flags.

All frames have the same structure:

  • Flag at the start and at the end.
  • Address (8 bits): meaningful in the unbalanced configuration, with several secondaries on a bus. Between two combined stations the value is fixed and irrelevant: there is only one possible peer.
  • Control (8 or 16 bits): variable format; flow control and link control are implemented on top of it.
  • Data: variable length, transparent and code-independent.
  • FCS (16 or 32 bits): a CRC computed over the bits of the frame, without the flags.
If the FCS computed by the receiver does not match, the frame is ignored: for the protocol it is the same as if it had been lost.
The control field: I, S, and U frames

The first bits indicate the frame type:

  • I · Information (0): carries data, with N(S) and N(R).
  • S · Supervisory (10): flow and error control. RR receiver ready, RNR receiver not ready, REJ simple reject, SREJ selective reject (rarely used).
  • U · Unnumbered (11): connection and disconnection. SABM requests a connection, UA acknowledges, DISC closes, DM refuses the connection, FRMR rejects a frame.

The P/F bit is in all three: in a command it is Poll (demands a response) and in the response it is Final.
N(R) = 4 means: I received everything correctly up to 3, I expect 4.

N(S): number of the frame I am sending. N(R): number of the frame I expect, like the TCP ACK, but they count frames, not bytes. With 3 bits, numbering is modulo 8 (0 to 7). With a 16-bit control field they become 7 bits: modulo 128, window of up to 127 frames.

HDLC is connection-oriented. Either end can initiate it with an unnumbered SABM frame (asynchronous balanced mode), which also sets whether numbering uses 3 or 7 bits (in that case, SABME).

When it is sent, timer T1 starts: if it expires with no response, the frame is retransmitted. After N attempts the link is declared unavailable.

The other end accepts with UA or refuses with DM.

Disconnection is abrupt: DISC and UA. It is not like TCP, where each side closes its own half: I frames pending acknowledgment can be lost.
U frames are called unnumbered because they carry neither N(S) nor N(R).
Example I: data in both directions

Each information frame is written I, N(S), N(R).

  • A sends I,0,0. B responds with its own data, I,0,1: its frame 0 and, riding on top, the acknowledgment of A's 0. This is piggybacking.
  • A sends 1 and 2. B waits until it has something to send and with I,1,3 acknowledges both together: the acknowledgment is cumulative, as in TCP.
  • At the end A receives B's 2 and 3 and has no data. So that B's T1 does not expire and trigger a retransmission, it acknowledges with a supervisory frame: RR,4.
If there is data to send, the acknowledgment travels in the same I frame; if not, an RR is used.

B sends I,3,0. A receives it, but needs to temporarily stop transmission: it activates flow control with RNR,4. It acknowledges 3 and signals that it is not ready; even if B has credit, it must not send more.

If B needs to transmit and the link is still suspended, it polls A with RR,0,P: the Poll bit demands a response.

A replies with the Final bit: RNR,4,F while it is still busy, RR,4,F when it is ready. Only then does B send I,4,0.
P goes in the command and F in the response: a poll always gets an answer.

A sends I,3,0, I,4,0, and I,5,0. Frame 4 is lost: for example, it arrives with a bad FCS and B discards it. A does not know and keeps sending.

B receives 3 and then 5: an out-of-sequence frame. It sends REJ,4: reject, I expect 4.

A goes back to 4 and transmits from there on (4, 5, and 6), regardless of the fact that 5 had already arrived. This is go-back-N, the simple reject.

The alternative is selective reject, SREJ, which requests a single frame: more efficient, but much more complex.
REJ,N: retransmission starts from frame N onward.

A sends 2 and 3. Frame 3 is lost or arrives with an error.

B can only acknowledge what it received. Since it has nothing to send, it uses a supervisory frame: RR,3 (I got 2, I expect 3).

A keeps waiting for the acknowledgment of 3 and T1 expires. Before retransmitting it polls B with RR,0,P, and B answers RR,3,F: it is up and running and communication can continue.

Then A retransmits I,3,0 and B acknowledges with RR,4.
There is no REJ here because no other frame arrived after the lost one: it is the timer that triggers recovery.

• WAN data link protocol, bit-oriented and connection-oriented; today used between combined stations.
  • The 7E flag delimits frames and zero insertion makes them transparent.
  • Control field: I frames, S (RR, RNR, REJ, SREJ) and U (SABM, UA, DISC, DM).
  • N(S) and N(R) count frames, modulo 8 or 128; the P/F bit polls.
  • Recovery uses REJ (go-back-N) or timer T1.

HDLC acknowledges and retransmits on every link. In the next lesson, Frame Relay inherits its frame but stops recovering from errors: it connects remote sites with virtual circuits over a shared network.
I, N(S), N(R): I send my frame N(S) and expect your frame N(R). Acknowledgments are cumulative and count frames, not bytes.

011111010: a 0 is inserted after five consecutive 1s
An escape character followed by the flag
The sender inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s, without looking at what follows; the receiver removes it and recovers the message.
A station receives an I frame with N(R) = 4. What is the other end telling it?
That it has 4 frames left to send
That it received everything correctly up to frame 3 and expects 4
N(R) is the number of the next expected frame: it cumulatively acknowledges all previous ones, and it counts frames, not bytes.
B receives frame 3 and then 5. With simple reject, what happens?
B sends SREJ,4 and A retransmits only 4
B sends RNR,4 and A stops
B sends REJ,4 and A retransmits from 4 onward
B waits for its timer T1 to expire
REJ triggers go-back-N: A goes back to frame 4 and retransmits from there, even though 5 had already arrived.
Why does a station send an RR frame with the P bit set?
To poll the other end and demand a response, which arrives with the F bit
To indicate it is the last data frame
P (Poll) in a command demands a response; the other end answers with F (Final). It is used when the link is suspended or before retransmitting after T1 expires.
01111110 (7E): marks the start and end of every frame.
The sender adds a 0 after five consecutive 1s; the receiver removes it. This way the flag never appears inside the message.
